title: Explainer
summary: Explain an idea, concept, process or data set with a voice, diagrams that build and a worked example: educational video, lesson, data story, 30 s to several minutes.

notFor.when: the request is how to use a specific product, app or website step by step (tutorial, walkthrough, onboarding)
an animated film whose point is the motion and type, not teaching an idea (kinetic typography, logo, music-driven, abstract)
the user recorded the lesson themselves and wants it cut, captioned or reframed
a generated presenter, avatar or talking photo delivers the explanation to camera

alternatives.when: a source-backed lesson from supplied originals (narration, images or video, source files) with chapters and timed captions; nothing is designed or generated

qa: A concrete worked example comes before each general rule, formula or definition
Text inside the picture is labels of one to three words beside the part they name, not the narration printed out (captions are a separate layer)
Narration pace measured from the voice with speech:local and recorded in the project
The film ends on a retrieval question or prediction the viewer answers before the answer is shown, not on a recap alone
Each segment answers one question and runs under 6 minutes; a longer film is chaptered

intake.ask: Which question does the film answer, in the words your audience would ask it?
intake.why: The question is the proposition and each segment answers one; without it there is no structure.

intake.ask: Which sources back it: papers, articles, notes or data files I can read?
intake.why: Every number and causal claim needs a status in the truth step; with no source it stops and names what it needs.

intake.ask: What does the viewer already know, and which terms are new to them?
intake.why: New terms are named and shown before use (pre-training); known ones are not explained again.
intake.default: A curious adult with no training in the field

intake.ask: How long, and where will it be shown: YouTube, a course, a site, a talk or a deck?
intake.why: Placement sets length, chapters, captions and the ending (profiles); a film in a talk has no call to action.

intake.ask: Is there a look or a visual metaphor to keep, such as a brand or a series style?
intake.why: One metaphor and one look hold through the film and a series.
intake.default: The design-director proposes one metaphor and proves it on the hardest diagram

profiles.note: Segments under 6 min (Guo et al.); longer films are chaptered: first timestamp 00:00, three or more chapters, each at least 10 s. SRT sidecar for the upload.
One idea or one chart as a post or in-stream ad (90 s cap; 15-30 s fits every feed placement); SRT captions text only; LinkedIn lists less than 30 fps: verify at upload.
Page or course embed: autoplay is muted, so captions are burned or the player's track is on; Wistia engagement holds from 1 to 5 min and falls after.
Plays in a deck or behind a speaker: no burned captions unless it plays silent, no call to action, the last diagram state holds as the slide. Length band is a house rule, a starting point.

starter.note: A change, a trend and the one number to remember, with labels that build beside the part they name. warm-editorial suits essays and education with long holds; a brand or series look overrides it.

variants.title: Data story or report video
variants.changes: A data file is a required source (--product data.json or .csv). Each on-screen number states subject, period and basis, with a source line. One chart is carried through its states (layout carry) with data blocks; chart:inspect checks charts against their records in workflow and template projects. The story is what changed and why; it ends on the one number to remember (hero-stat-odometer).

variants.title: Designed course lesson
variants.changes: A designed, animated lesson in a series (a lesson the user filmed is footage-edit). The learning objective is stated in the first 10 s; prerequisite terms come first; 3-6 min per lesson; each lesson ends on a retrieval question, a held pause, then the answer. Chapters planned in the beat sheet (video:longform assembles them when built through the education workflow); captions plus SRT for the course platform; one look and one recap pattern across the series.
